title: The Complete Peru Travel Guide
subtitle: Lost Inca cities, high-altitude lakes and desert oases across one of South America's most dramatic landscapes
summary: How to plan a Peru trip: whether to focus on the Andes, the coast or the Amazon, when to go for the driest trails, what it costs, and a practical ten-day itinerary.

sections.title: How Peru divides
body: Peru genuinely divides into three very different geographic zones — the coast, the Andean highlands and the Amazon — and a first trip realistically covers only one or two well.

**The Andean highlands.** [[cusco|Cusco]], [[machu-picchu|Machu Picchu]], the [[sacred-valley|Sacred Valley]], [[rainbow-mountain|Rainbow Mountain]] and [[lake-titicaca-puno|Lake Titicaca]] — the historic and scenic heart of most Peru itineraries.
**The coast.** [[lima|Lima]], [[nazca-lines|the Nazca Lines]] and [[huacachina|Huacachina]] — the capital's food scene and a strip of desert coastline with its own distinct attractions.
**The south.** [[arequipa-colca-canyon|Arequipa and Colca Canyon]] — a genuinely underrated colonial city and one of the world's deepest canyons.
**The Amazon.** [[amazon-puerto-maldonado|Puerto Maldonado]] — a genuinely different Peru entirely, dense rainforest and extraordinary biodiversity.
sections.note: Most first-time visitors genuinely combine [[lima|Lima]] with the Andean highlands in a single trip. The Amazon and the far south coast are where a longer or second trip belongs.

list.title: If this is your first trip
list.text: [[lima|Lima]], [[cusco|Cusco]], the [[sacred-valley|Sacred Valley]] and [[machu-picchu|Machu Picchu]], genuinely the classic route for a reason.

list.title: If you want dramatic high-altitude scenery
list.text: [[rainbow-mountain|Rainbow Mountain]], genuinely one of the most photographed natural sights in the Andes.

list.title: If you want living Andean culture
list.text: [[lake-titicaca-puno|Lake Titicaca]], home to the Uros floating islands and Taquile's weaving traditions.

list.title: If you want an underrated colonial city
list.text: [[arequipa-colca-canyon|Arequipa]], genuinely one of Peru's most beautiful cities, paired with condor-watching at Colca Canyon.

list.title: If you want extraordinary wildlife
list.text: [[amazon-puerto-maldonado|The Amazon]], genuinely one of the most biodiverse places on Earth.

list.title: If you want something different from the Andes
list.text: [[nazca-lines|The Nazca Lines]] and [[huacachina|Huacachina]], genuinely a striking desert detour on Peru's southern coast.

sections.title: Getting around: flights, trains, and one common mistake
body: Peru's scale and mountainous terrain genuinely mean no single mode of transport covers the whole country — a mix of domestic flights, trains and buses is standard.
**Fly between regions, don't drive.** [[lima|Lima]] to [[cusco|Cusco]] or [[arequipa-colca-canyon|Arequipa]] genuinely takes over 24 hours by road versus about an hour and a half by air.
**Book the Machu Picchu train well ahead.** It's genuinely the only practical way to reach [[machu-picchu|Machu Picchu]] without a multi-day hike.
**Don't skip altitude acclimatisation.** Arriving in [[cusco|Cusco]] at 3,400 metres and rushing straight into activity is genuinely the most common mistake first-time visitors make.
**Use overnight buses for longer coastal routes.** [[nazca-lines|Nazca]] to [[huacachina|Ica]] and similar routes are genuinely comfortable on Peru's reclining-seat overnight services.
**Book Rainbow Mountain and Colca Canyon tours locally.** Both genuinely involve early starts and high-altitude driving best left to experienced operators.
sections.note: Book your Machu Picchu tickets, train and Inca Trail permits (if hiking) months ahead for June–August travel — Peru's dry season genuinely sells out early.

sections.title: When to go
body: Peru's three distinct regions genuinely have different ideal seasons, so 'the best time' depends on where your itinerary focuses. For the classic Andean route, **May to September** works best.
**The Andean dry season** brings genuinely reliable weather for Machu Picchu, Cusco and Rainbow Mountain, also the busiest and most expensive season.
**The wet season**, November to March, is genuinely lush and green, though trails can turn muddy and the Inca Trail itself closes each February.
**The Amazon's own dry season**, roughly June to October, genuinely offers the easiest wildlife spotting, with lower water levels concentrating animals near rivers.
**The coast**, including Lima and the desert south, is genuinely mild year-round, with its own separate garúa fog season affecting Lima specifically from June to September.
sections.note: Book Machu Picchu tickets and Inca Trail permits (if hiking) many months ahead for a June–August trip — this is genuinely the busiest and most tightly booked window of the year.

list.title: Six days: the highlights sprint
list.text: [[lima|Lima]], [[cusco|Cusco]] and [[machu-picchu|Machu Picchu]], genuinely the most popular short Peru itinerary, though tight on acclimatisation time.
list.tip: Fly into Cusco a day earlier than needed if possible, purely for extra altitude adjustment time.

list.title: Ten days: the classic Andean loop
list.text: The itinerary on the [[c:peru|Peru country page]]: [[lima|Lima]], [[cusco|Cusco]], the [[sacred-valley|Sacred Valley]], [[machu-picchu|Machu Picchu]], [[rainbow-mountain|Rainbow Mountain]] and [[lake-titicaca-puno|Lake Titicaca]]. A genuinely complete first look at Peru's classic highlights.
list.tip: Do Rainbow Mountain only after at least three days at altitude — it's a genuinely serious high-altitude hike.

list.title: A week focused on the south
list.text: [[arequipa-colca-canyon|Arequipa and Colca Canyon]] paired with [[nazca-lines|Nazca]] and [[huacachina|Huacachina]], skipping Cusco entirely.
list.tip: This route genuinely avoids the highest altitudes, a good option for those concerned about altitude sickness.

list.title: An Amazon add-on for a second trip
list.text: [[amazon-puerto-maldonado|Puerto Maldonado]] by guided lodge stay, genuinely one of the most biodiverse regions on Earth.
list.tip: Book a genuinely multi-night lodge stay rather than a single day trip — wildlife sightings improve significantly with more time.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Peru?
faq.a: Ten to fourteen days covers Lima, Cusco, the Sacred Valley, Machu Picchu and Lake Titicaca at a reasonable pace, which is the itinerary in this guide. Six days is enough for the highlights alone, and genuinely still worthwhile.

faq.q: Is Machu Picchu worth the cost and effort?
faq.a: Yes, genuinely — it's one of the only major ancient wonders the Spanish conquest never found, and no photograph quite captures standing in the citadel itself.

faq.q: Do you need to worry about altitude in Peru?
faq.a: Yes, genuinely, in Cusco and Puno especially — both sit above 3,300 metres, and rushing straight into activity without acclimatising is the most common visitor mistake.

faq.q: When should I visit for the best weather?
faq.a: May to September for the Andean dry season, offering the most reliable conditions for Machu Picchu, Cusco and Rainbow Mountain, though it's also the busiest and priciest time to visit.
